newsitem.title: USA: Colombia seeks coordinated Latam oil exports to US.
newsitem.headline: Colombia seeks coordinated Latam oil exports to US.

text.p: Colombian Energy and Mines Minister Rodrigo Villamizar on Tuesday said he plans to call on counterparts in Mexico and Venezuela to coordinate policies on oil and natural gas exports to the United States.

In an interview in Houston with Reuters, Villamizar said he planned to ask the countries to "join efforts in proposing a future policy on oil, oil exploration and production, exports and the usage and utilization of gas."

"The only one who is suggesting that we coordinate policies towards, specifically related to, the United States, is Colombia to this point," he said. "All the other two countries have said is 'it's interesting.'"

The proposal came as President Bill Clinton considers imposing punitive sanctions on Colombia after decertifying the country last year for falling short in its fight against drugs and drug trafficking.

Decertification for a second consecutive year could trigger U.S. commercial sanctions against Colombia, which has been courting foreign investment to boost oil and gas production and privatize its electric industry.

Villamizar said his proposal to coordinate oil exports has found some measure of support among energy and foreign affairs ministers in Venezuela and Mexico, two of the four largest suppliers of crude oil to the United States.

Venezuela in the first half of last year was the leading exporter to the United States, supplying 1.6 million barrels per day or more than 17 percent of total imports, while Mexico was the fourth leading importer at 1.23 million barrels per day, the American Petroleum Institute said.

Colombia, meanwhile, is seeking to boost production to 920,000 barrels per day in 1998 from current production of 620,000 barrels per day and build reserves to 15 billion barrels in the next 50 years, up from 3.5 billion barrels today.
"Most of the energy resources of the continent today are in the hands of three countries outside of the United States - Mexico, Venezuela and Colombia," Villamizar said.
